items.mnemonic_text: A single horizontal stroke is the ground floor: one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look down at the ground: it's a single flat line stretching out in front of you, nothing else. Just that one unbroken stroke, flat and simple. One line, one ground, the number one.
items.reading_mnemonic: A little kid named Ichi is so proud he can finally count, and he keeps holding up one finger and shouting 「いち！」 at everyone who passes. That single raised finger is his whole personality — he only knows number one.
items.description: Means "one" and is the simplest kanji you'll meet, a single horizontal stroke; it shows up everywhere numbers appear, from counting to dates.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と一緒に海に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to the sea with a friend tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に海[うみ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝ご飯にパンを一つ食べました。
example_sentences.english: I ate one piece of bread for breakfast.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]にパンを一[いち]つ食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 水が一番安いです。
example_sentences.english: Water is the cheapest.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[みず]が一[いち]番[ばん]安[やす]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Two stacked strokes count out two.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you'll see two flat lines stacked on top of each other, one short, one long. Two lines, nothing more. That's two.
items.reading_mnemonic: A knee (に) buckles under you right as you climb the second of the two flat lines — you can only ever bend one knee at a time, but here you need two. Every time you slip on those stacked lines, you land on your に.
items.description: The kanji for "two" (the number 2), drawn as two stacked horizontal lines; shows up everywhere numbers do, like dates, counting, and prices.

example_sentences.japanese: これを二つ買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll buy two of these.
example_sentences.furigana: これを二[に]つ買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 二日、犬と遊びました。
example_sentences.english: I played with a dog for two days.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]日[ひ]、犬[いぬ]と遊[あそ]びました。

example_sentences.japanese: 二十日に彼女が来ます。
example_sentences.english: She is coming on the twentieth.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]十[じゅう]日[ひ]に彼[かの]女[じょ]が来[らい]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: Three stacked strokes: one, two, three.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and count what you see: three flat lines stacked neatly on top of each other. One line, then another, then a third. Three lines means, simply, three.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful ranch hand named San lines up three fence rails on the mountain trail, tapping each one and calling out 「さん」 as she checks the count. Three rails, three, and San says the number every time.
items.description: The kanji for three, the number 3, appearing constantly in counting, dates, and prices.

example_sentences.japanese: 三時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: I wake up at three o'clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: パンを三つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought three loaves of bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを三[さん]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで三日待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait here for three days.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで三[さん]日[ひ]待[ま]ちます。

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth boxing in legs that kick four ways: four.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You peer into the closed box of the enclosure, walls all around, and inside you find a mouth trapped in the corner. It sits there counting on its lips, and the number it keeps landing on is four. An enclosure with a mouth inside: four.
items.reading_mnemonic: Inside those walls, a tiny shopkeeper named Shi is stacking exactly four onigiri and hissing "し, し, し" as she counts. Every time she runs out of breath, she's counted to four.
items.description: The kanji for four, the number 4, used constantly for counting, dates, prices, and phone numbers.

example_sentences.japanese: パンを四つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought four pieces of bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを四[よん]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 四日に友達に会います。
example_sentences.english: I will meet my friend on the fourth.
example_sentences.furigana: 四[よん]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: これは四ですか？
example_sentences.english: Is this a four?
example_sentences.furigana: これは四[よん]ですか？

items.mnemonic_text: A shape crossing itself, the hand held up: five fingers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and picture a hook or a hand reaching sideways to snag things off a shelf. Now imagine you're grabbing snacks that way — one, two, three, four, and with that last crooked pull you land your fifth. That little hooked shape is you catching five things in one swipe.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kid counting up his catch is Go, and once he hits five he throws his hands up and yells "ご!" like it's the winning number. Every time he lands a fifth thing, out comes that triumphant ご.
items.description: The kanji for five, the number 5, seen everywhere from prices and dates to counting and phone numbers.

example_sentences.japanese: パンを五つ買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy five pieces of bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを五[ご]つ買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、五時に学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to school at five tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、五[ご]時[じ]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は五日待ちました。
example_sentences.english: He waited for five days.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は五[ご]日[ひ]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: A little hat on two legs stands over six.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the number eight standing tall, and then set a little lid right on top of it. That lid caps the eight and knocks it down two — from eight, you drop to six. The lid on top of eight always means six.
items.reading_mnemonic: A rock star climbs onto the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and belts out six songs to the empty air. Every time he screams "ろく!" a cat appears, until six of them are yowling backup. That rock (ろく) show is how you hear six.
items.description: Means six; the basic number 6, seen everywhere from counting and prices to dates and times.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今日六時に起きました。
example_sentences.english: I got up at six o'clock today.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今日[きょう]六[ろく]時[じ]に起[お]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋にパンが六つあります。
example_sentences.english: There are six pieces of bread in this room.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]にパンが六[ろく]つあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 六日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to watch a movie with my friend on the 6th.
example_sentences.furigana: 六[ろく]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: A slanted cross like a scythe cutting seven.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the whole character: a single upright stroke with a long arm sweeping across it, like a bent nail hammered halfway into a wall and then hooked to hang something on. Picture yourself hanging exactly seven coats on that one crooked hook by the door. When it bends under all that weight, you know it's holding seven.
items.reading_mnemonic: A shy cat at Grandma Kane's shrine will only come out when you call it exactly seven times — and each time you call, you shush the other cats: しち, しち, quiet now. By the seventh しち, it finally pads down the mossy steps.
items.description: The kanji for seven (7), used constantly in counting, dates, prices, and telling time.

example_sentences.english: I will go to school on the seventh.

example_sentences.english: I bought seven pieces of bread today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、パンを七[なな]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、七時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: I will wake up at seven o'clock tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、七[なな]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Two strokes spreading apart like the number eight opening up.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at those two strokes leaning away from each other, spreading apart at the bottom like legs mid-stride. They're splitting, opening wider and wider — and the wider they split, the bigger the number gets. That spread lands you on eight.
items.reading_mnemonic: A honeybee — a はち in Japanese — drifts down to the onigiri shelf in Koichi's konbini and lands on exactly eight of them, one after another. You count the buzzing little はち as it goes: eight stops, eight onigiri.
items.description: Means "eight" (the number 8); appears in counting and in dates and times like 八時 (eight o'clock).

example_sentences.japanese: ここに八を書きます。
example_sentences.english: I will write an eight here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここに八[はち]を書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、パンを八つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought eight pieces of bread yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、パンを八[はち]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 八日に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'm meeting a friend on the eighth.
example_sentences.furigana: 八[はち]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

items.mnemonic_text: A hook curling back at the top of the count: nine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and see a hook curling forward, the kind of cane you'd hang up after a long day. Picture yourself at the bottom of the mountain trail, counting the switchbacks left before the top: one, two, all the way up to that last brutal bend that looks exactly like this hooked shape. You lean on your cane at bend nine, and that curl is the number nine.
items.reading_mnemonic: At bend nine on the mountain trail you finally reach the vending machine, but your legs give out — you go "きゅう!" as you collapse against it. That sharp little cry of relief at spot nine is exactly the sound きゅう.
items.description: Means "nine," the number 9; shows up constantly in counting, dates, and prices.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、パンを九つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought nine pieces of bread yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、パンを九[きゅう]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、学生が九人来ました。
example_sentences.english: Nine students came today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、学[がく]生[せい]が九[きゅう]人[ひと]来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで彼を九日待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for him here for nine days.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで彼[かれ]を九[きゅう]日[ひ]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: A perfect plus sign, fingers of both hands: ten.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you see one perfect plus sign, one clean cross. That plus sign is the mark you use when you count all the way up to a full set on your fingers — two hands, all of them raised. A single cross standing tall like this means ten.
items.reading_mnemonic: A judo champion bursts into Koichi's konbini and slaps down exactly ten coins on the beeping till, shouting じゅう with each one. Every time you picture that plus-sign cross, hear the judo master's じゅう ringing out.
items.description: Means ten (the number 10); one of the first counting kanji and a building block for larger numbers like 十一 and 二十.

example_sentences.japanese: これを十買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy ten of these.
example_sentences.furigana: これを十[じゅう]買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 十日に家へ帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I will go home on the 10th.
example_sentences.furigana: 十[じゅう]日[ひ]に家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]ります。

example_sentences.english: I will write from one to ten.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から十[じゅう]まで書[か]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: One (一) over a white (白) sheet counted a hundred times.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Put the number one on top of a ray of light so bright it turns white, and look what happens: that single one stacked over the white glow multiplies into a whole crowd. One little stroke sitting above all that whiteness isn't just one anymore — it's a hundred.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a hiccuping cook keeps counting onigiri, and every time he hits a full tray he lets out a huge "ひゃく!" — a hiccup and a yell in one, because a hundred rice balls is a lot to hiccup through.
items.description: The kanji for "hundred" (100), which shows up constantly in prices, counting, and numbers like 三百.

example_sentences.japanese: 一から百まで書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote from one to one hundred.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から百[ひゃく]まで書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が百人来ました。
example_sentences.english: A hundred students came.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が百[ひゃく]人[ひと]来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 本を百買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a hundred books.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]を百[ひゃく]買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A slash over ten (十) multiplies it into a thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take the plus sign for ten and lay a single slash across its top, like one bold pen-stroke scratched over it. That one extra mark turns humble ten into something enormous — you've just multiplied it a hundredfold. Ten with a lid on top means a thousand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A senator named Sen shows up at the shrine and drops a thousand coins into the offering box all at once. "That's from all my constituents," she says, "せん of them exactly." Every time you see this kanji, hear Sen bragging about her せん coins.
items.description: Means thousand (1000); the counter you'll see constantly in prices, dates, and big round numbers.

example_sentences.japanese: 一から千まで書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote from one to one thousand.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から千[せん]まで書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が千人来ました。
example_sentences.english: A thousand students came.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が千[せん]人[ひと]来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 千の魚を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw a thousand fish.
example_sentences.furigana: 千[せん]の魚[さかな]を見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A single hooked mark standing for a whole ten thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook-shaped banner snapping in the wind above a market stall. On that one banner, someone has painted a running tally that just keeps climbing — past a thousand, past nine thousand, until the whole cloth is crammed with zeros. That one impossibly loaded banner stands for ten thousand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A street vendor named Manny throws his arms wide under that banner and yells, "Man, I've sold ten thousand of these!" You can hear the まん right there in his ecstatic "Man!" as the crowd surges in.
items.description: Means "ten thousand" and shows up constantly in prices, populations, and big round numbers like 万円 (ten thousand yen).

example_sentences.japanese: 一から万まで書きます。
example_sentences.english: I'll write from one to ten thousand.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から万[まん]まで書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が一万人来ました。
example_sentences.english: Ten thousand students came.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が一[いち]万[まん]人[ひと]来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 一万の本があります。
example_sentences.english: There are ten thousand books.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]万[まん]の本[ほん]があります。

items.mnemonic_text: A boxed shape holding the round yen coin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character straight on: it's a rounded box, a coin flattened into a frame. Picture a single shiny coin held tight inside a square window, so perfectly round it's almost a circle. That coin is a yen, and its round shape is the circle.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the beeping till spits out change, and a friend named En scoops up every round coin, grinning "these えん are mine." Every time you hear the till beep, picture En pocketing えん.
items.description: Means yen (Japan's currency) and also circle or round; shows up on money, prices, and words for round shapes.

example_sentences.japanese: この本は千円でした。
example_sentences.english: This book was a thousand yen.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は千[せん]円[えん]でした。

example_sentences.english: The coffee is three hundred yen, and cheap.
example_sentences.furigana: コーヒーは三[さん]百[びゃく]円[えん]で、安[やす]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あの映画は千五百円で、高いです。
example_sentences.english: That movie is fifteen hundred yen, which is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: あの映[えい]画[が]は千[せん]五[ご]百[ひゃく]円[えん]で、高[たか]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A window with a line: the sun rising to mark the day.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the character: it's a window with a bar across the middle. Through that window you can see the sun climbing into the sky, and once the sun is up, a whole new day begins. Window plus bar, sun in the frame — that's a day.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat wakes at dawn and greets the rising sun with the same cry every morning: "にち! にち!" The others answer, and that's how the whole shrine knows a new day has started.
items.description: Means "day" or "sun"; one of the most common kanji, showing up in dates, days of the week, and countless everyday words.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: Today I'm watching a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.english: I speak Japanese every day.

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日に海へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: On Sunday I'm going to the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A crescent with two lines: the moon marking each month.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look up on a clear night and there it is: a thin crescent hanging in the dark, the moon. Watch that crescent fatten, fade, and swing back around, and you've just watched one whole month go by. This character is that crescent — so it means moon, and it means month.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gecko has claimed the moon as its own, scuttling across the crescent every night. Whenever it does, you hear its little feet go げつ, げつ against the pale surface. That gecko-on-the-moon sound is how you remember げつ.
items.description: Means moon or month; a common kanji that shows up in dates, days of the week (Monday), and countless month-related words.

example_sentences.english: I'll meet a friend next month.

example_sentences.english: I'm looking at the moon right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、月[つき]を見[み]ています。

example_sentences.japanese: 月曜日に学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school on Monday.
example_sentences.furigana: 月[げつ]曜[よう]日[ひ]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A person with sparks flying off each side: fire.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with their arms flung out, and sparks are flying off them in every direction. They're crackling, glowing, throwing off heat — this is a person who has become fire. Every time you see 火, see that sparking figure and think: fire.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and lets out a puff of flame with a raspy caw: 「か!」. The flame and the sound arrive together, so when you see this fire kanji, you hear Kaa's か.
items.description: Means "fire"; a very common N5 kanji found in everyday words for flame, fire, and even Tuesday (火曜日).

example_sentences.english: On Tuesday I'm watching a movie with a friend.

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の火曜日はとても忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: Next Tuesday I'm really busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]はとても忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 火曜日の朝、公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Tuesday morning, I'm going to the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]の朝[あさ]、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Streams splashing out from a central flow: water.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Stand at the riverbank and watch the streams splashing outward in every direction, cold spray hitting your face. Those wild, branching streaks are the whole picture: water.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a swimmer named Sui dives in and shouts "すい!" as the cold hits, then keeps splashing everyone within reach. Every time you see this kanji, hear Sui hollering すい from the water.
items.description: Means "water"; a very common kanji that shows up in everyday words for water, drinks, and Wednesday (水曜日).

example_sentences.japanese: 暑いから、水を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: It's hot, so I'll drink some water.
example_sentences.furigana: 暑[あつ]いから、水[みず]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Wednesday I'll watch a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝、水を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: Every morning I drink water.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]、水[みず]を飲[の]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A trunk with roots and branches: a tree.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character and you can see it whole: a single vertical trunk, roots digging down at the bottom and branches reaching out to the sides. Stand back and the shape is unmistakable — a tree.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles as she climbs to the very top and peeks over the leaves — she's playing "もく" (peekaboo), disappearing behind branches every time the wind blows. Whenever you spot this tree, hear her whisper もく from up in the canopy.
items.description: Means "tree"; a very common N5 kanji that appears in nature words and, on its own, refers to a tree.

example_sentences.japanese: 木曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Thursday I'm watching a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの木はとても高いです。
example_sentences.english: That tree over there is really tall.
example_sentences.furigana: あの木[き]はとても高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎週木曜日に学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school every Thursday.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]週[しゅう]木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a mountain of buried gold and money.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a solid little roof, and buried right underneath it, a stash of gleaming nuggets you'd never leave lying around. That roof over buried nuggets is exactly what this character shows you: precious metal tucked away safe. Dig it up and you've got gold and money.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her real fortune under the shrine's giant bell, and every time a cat brushes it, it goes きん. That soft きん ring is the sound of gold sitting safe underneath.
items.description: Means gold or money; a very common kanji you'll see in prices, banks (金曜日 for Friday too), and anything valuable.

example_sentences.japanese: 金曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Friday I'll watch a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: お金がないから、今日は家に帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I don't have any money, so I'm going home today.
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]がないから、今日[きょう]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 現金でご飯を買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll pay for the meal in cash.
example_sentences.furigana: 現[げん]金[きん]でご飯[はん]を買[か]います。

items.mnemonic_text: A cross pushed into the ground: earth and soil.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a simple cross being pushed straight down into the ground, staking out a plot of dirt. The moment its base sinks in, the loose brown stuff piles up around it. That cross pressed into the ground is earth, plain soil.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gardener drops to his knees in the plot and starts digging with his bare hands, going "do, do, do" (ど) as he flings soil over his shoulder. Every heavy handful he tosses out lands with that same low ど grunt.
items.description: Means earth or soil; shows up in words about ground, land, and even Saturday (土曜日).

example_sentences.japanese: 土曜日に公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the park on Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎週土曜日に海へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the sea every Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]週[しゅう]土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今週の土曜日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy this Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]週[しゅう]の土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Three peaks rising up: a mountain range.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape and count them: three peaks rising side by side, the middle one tallest. You don't need a story here — the character is a picture. Those three peaks are a mountain.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine has a face, and it greets every exhausted hiker like an old friend: "You made it — welcome, san (さん)!" It calls everyone さん because on this mountain, reaching the peak earns you respect.
items.description: Means "mountain"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place and family names.

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は高いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain is high.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末、友達と山に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the mountains with a friend on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]、友[とも]達[だち]と山[やま]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の写真はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is the photo of the mountain?
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の写[しゃ]真[しん]はどこですか。

items.mnemonic_text: Three flowing lines of a running river.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and squint: three flowing lines running side by side down the page. That's water moving — three currents carving their way through the land. Three flowing lines: a river.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank you meet a fisherman who has cast a line into every one of those three currents. He grins and tells you he's caught a thousand — せん — fish today, one for each ripple in the river.
items.description: Means "river"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place names.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、川に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to the river today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、川[かわ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、友達と一緒に川で遊びました。
example_sentences.english: I played by the river with my friend yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に川[かわ]で遊[あそ]びました。

example_sentences.japanese: 川で魚を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw a fish in the river.
example_sentences.furigana: 川[かわ]で魚[さかな]を見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (大) with a line above their head: the heavens.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a stick figure standing with arms flung wide, and then a long flat line laid across the very top of them — a ceiling stretched over the whole world. That line above everyone's outstretched arms is the ceiling of everything: the heaven, the sky.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tent-pitcher hikes to the top of the mountain trail and, instead of camping on the ground, throws a giant tent (てん) up into the air to sleep among the clouds. When you crane your neck at the sky, you spot that tent (てん) floating right there in heaven.
items.description: Means heaven or sky; a common N5 kanji that shows up in words about weather and the heavens.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はいい天気ですね。
example_sentences.english: The weather is nice today, isn't it?
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]はいい天[てん]気[き]ですね。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は天気がいいですか。
example_sentences.english: Will the weather be nice tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は天[てん]気[き]がいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日は天気が良かったです。
example_sentences.english: The weather was good yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]は天[てん]気[き]が良[よ]かったです。

items.mnemonic_text: Steam rising with an X inside: the invisible energy or mood.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a little puff of steam curling up off a hot bowl of rice — that swirling, rising shape is exactly this character. You can almost see the wisp lifting into the air, alive and moving. That invisible thing rising off warm things is the very idea of spirit and energy.
items.reading_mnemonic: The steam curls up and out pops Kiki, the tree spirit, giggling as the wind stirs her branches. She rides that rising energy on a breeze of 「き」.
items.description: Means spirit or energy; a very common kanji found in words about mood, feeling, weather, and vitality.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は元気ですか。
example_sentences.english: Are you feeling well today?
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は元[げん]気[き]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の犬は病気です。
example_sentences.english: My dog is sick.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の犬[いぬ]は病[びょう]気[き]です。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は気持ちがいいです。
example_sentences.english: This room feels nice.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は気[き]持[も]ちがいいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Grass on top of a person changing (化): a blooming flower.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single tall stem topped by a wide, open bloom leaning to one side, its petals spilling over the edge of the pot. That whole leaning shape is the character: stem below, blossom bursting out above. Every time you see it, you're looking at a flower.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands right in the middle of the flowerbed and lets out a proud 「か」, singeing every petal within reach. Now the only flower left standing is the scorched one under her claws.
items.description: Means "flower"; a very common everyday kanji seen in words for flowers, plants, and blossoms.

example_sentences.japanese: 母に花を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought flowers for my mother.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]に花[はな]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で花を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw flowers at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で花[はな]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この花は高いです。
example_sentences.english: This flower is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は高[たか]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A mark sitting on top of a line: up and above.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single horizontal line — the ground — with a little mark standing tall right on top of it, reaching up into the air. Everything about this shape points one way: away from the ground and skyward. That thing sticking up above the line is exactly what it means — up, above.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful mountaineer plants her flag at the summit and shouts "Joe!" as she looks up at the sky — じょう rings out across the peak. Every time you look up and above you, you hear her じょう echoing back down.
items.description: Means "up" or "above"; a very common N5 kanji appearing in words for direction, position, and going up.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は話すのが上手です。
example_sentences.english: The teacher is good at speaking.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は話[はな]すのが上手[じょうず]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 本の上に猫が寝ています。
example_sentences.english: A cat is sleeping on the book.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]の上[うえ]に猫[ねこ]が寝[ね]ています。

example_sentences.japanese: 手を上げてください。
example_sentences.english: Please raise your hand.
example_sentences.furigana: 手[て]を上[あ]げてください。

items.mnemonic_text: A mark hanging under a line: down and below.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single horizontal shelf with a little mark hanging beneath it, dropping away toward the floor. Everything about the shape leans downward, pointing at the space under that shelf. That dangling tail tells you exactly where to look: down, below.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, dives straight down off the power line and lets out a sharp 「か」 as she plummets toward the ground below. Every time she drops down, that same caw of 「か」 rings out.
items.description: Means down or below; a very common kanji appearing in words about lower position, direction, and going down.

example_sentences.japanese: 本はあの窓の下です。
example_sentences.english: The book is under that window.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]はあの窓[まど]の下[した]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日地下鉄で学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school by subway every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]地[ち]下[か]鉄[てつ]で学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は話すのが下手です。
example_sentences.english: I'm not good at speaking.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は話[はな]すのが下手[へた]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A box speared straight through the middle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a mouth, that open square, and now imagine a single spear driven straight down through its center. The line splits the opening into two even halves, landing dead in the middle. Whatever you skewer that cleanly is right in the middle, tucked inside.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse, refuses to guard the door or the back — he plants himself squarely in the ちゅう, the very middle of the room, so no threat can slip past on either side. "The center is where a loyal mouse belongs," he squeaks.
items.description: Means middle or inside; extremely common, appearing in words about being in the middle of doing something, insides, and locations like the center of town.

example_sentences.japanese: みんな、中に入りました。
example_sentences.english: Everyone went inside.
example_sentences.furigana: みんな、中[なか]に入[い]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の真ん中に座りました。
example_sentences.english: I sat in the middle of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に座[すわ]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 家の中で本を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read a book inside the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]の中[なか]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person stretching arms and legs out wide: big.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with their arms flung out and their legs spread as wide as they can go, straining to show you just how huge the fish they caught was. That whole stretched-out stick figure is this character. When someone stands like that, they're always telling you one thing: it was big.
items.reading_mnemonic: The person is stretching so wide because they're measuring Dai, the giant baby, who is the size of a truck. You gasp だい as he cries an earthquake and you realize nothing has ever been this big.
items.description: Means "big"; a very common kanji found in everyday words for size, importance, and universities.

example_sentences.japanese: その犬は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: That dog is big.
example_sentences.furigana: その犬[いぬ]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、大学に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to the university tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、大[だい]学[がく]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: お母さんは大丈夫ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is your mother okay?
example_sentences.furigana: お母[はは]さんは大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: A tiny hook with two small dots: small.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single hook standing upright with two dots flanking it, one on each side, like something delicate pinched between two fingertips. It's so slight it could vanish if you sneezed. That tiny hook with its two little dots is the very picture of small.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, snaps his white glove and shrinks the whole set until the doves look like specks. As everything gets impossibly small, the crowd gasps, "しょう!" — the man himself is the smallest thing on stage.
items.description: Means "small" and shows up constantly in size words and compounds like 小学校; read しょう in compounds and ちい in 小さい.

example_sentences.japanese: あの小さい猫を見ましたか。
example_sentences.english: Did you see that small cat?
example_sentences.furigana: あの小[ちい]さい猫[ねこ]を見[み]ましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: My room is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の部屋[へや]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、小さい本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a small book yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、小[ちい]さい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a craftsman's tool, held in the left hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a carpenter's square held in a working hand, the arm braced hard so it doesn't slip while measuring. That steadying hand is doing the supporting job — the one that isn't the writing hand, the one on your other side. That's the hand on the left.
items.reading_mnemonic: A samurai marches into Koichi's konbini and slams down a coin with his left hand, barking "さ!" as he demands the last onigiri. Every time you see this kanji, hear that samurai's sharp さ ringing off the beeping till.
items.description: Means "left," the opposite of right; shows up constantly in directions and in the compound 左右 (left and right).

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は左です。
example_sentences.english: The station is on the left.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は左[ひだり]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 左に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go left.
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 左の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the left window.
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a mouth, the right hand that feeds you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a hand reaching down into an open mouth to pull something free — the fingers and the little box of the mouth locked together in one shape. That hand is always your dominant one, the one you shove in to grab a stuck snack. It's the hand on the right.
items.reading_mnemonic: You reach for the last onigiri on Koichi's shelf with your right hand and your fingers close on nothing but air, so you let out a soft "うう" of disappointment. That little "うう" is the sound you make when your right hand comes up empty.
items.description: Means "right" (the direction); appears constantly in directions and in words like right side and right hand.

example_sentences.japanese: トイレは右です。
example_sentences.english: The toilet is on the right.
example_sentences.furigana: トイレは右[みぎ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: ここから右に行きます。
example_sentences.english: We will go right from here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここから右[みぎ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 右の部屋で寝ます。
example_sentences.english: I sleep in the room on the right.
example_sentences.furigana: 右[みぎ]の部屋[へや]で寝[ね]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) tangled in a tree (木): sunrise in the east.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the sun rising and getting tangled in the branches of a tree on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's east.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "とう" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.
items.description: Means "east," the compass direction; shows up in place names like 東京 (Tokyo) and words for eastern directions.

example_sentences.japanese: 東の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I open the east window.
example_sentences.furigana: 東[ひがし]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の東で友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met a friend east of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の東[ひがし]で友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの町は東です。
example_sentences.english: That town is to the east.
example_sentences.furigana: あの町[まち]は東[ひがし]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A bird settling into its nest as the sun sets in the west.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a squat bird cage with a little bird perched inside, its legs dangling below the frame. At sunset the birds all fly home to roost, settling in the cage as the sun sinks in the same direction. That cage where everything comes to rest for the night points you toward the west.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, insists she always knows exactly where the sun sets, so she marches to the western edge of the sports field at dusk and points, calling out 「せい, that way!」 while the whole class watches the sky turn orange behind her.
items.description: Means west, one of the four compass directions; shows up in place names and words for western things and the western regions.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校は町の西です。
example_sentences.english: The school is in the west of the town.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]は町[まち]の西[にし]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は西から来ました。
example_sentences.english: He came from the west.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は西[にし]から来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは一緒に西へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: We went west together.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは一[いっ]緒[しょ]に西[にし]へ行[い]きました。

items.mnemonic_text: A warm shelter facing the sunny south.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character straight on and you'll see a little tent standing tall with a wind chime dangling under its roof. This is the tent you pitch on the warmest, sunniest patch of ground you can find — because you've dragged it all the way south, where the wind is soft enough to make that chime sing. Set up your tent and let it point you south.
items.reading_mnemonic: A backpacker named Nan has been hiking down the mountain trail for days, always heading south toward warmer weather. Every time someone asks which way she's going, she just points and sighs, "なん... south, always south." The word なん sticks because Nan won't stop saying it.
items.description: Means south; a compass direction that shows up in place names, directions, and words like 南口 (south exit).

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の南は海です。
example_sentences.english: South of the station is the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の南[みなみ]は海[うみ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は南の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the south window.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は南[みなみ]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は南から来ました。
example_sentences.english: He came from the south.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は南[みなみ]から来[らい]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: Two people back to back turning away from the cold north.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two people sitting back-to-back on a frozen bench, shoulders hunched against a bitter wind. That's the whole shape of this kanji — two figures turned away from each other, both refusing to face the cold gale howling down from the north. Whenever you see them sitting spine-to-spine like that, you know the icy wind is blowing from the north.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the wind off the northern peak is so brutal that a hiker named Hoku pulls his hood tight and mutters "ほく, ほく" through chattering teeth as he trudges. Hear him — ほく — every time you point north.
items.description: Means "north"; a common direction kanji that shows up in compass words and place names like 北 (north) and 北海道.

example_sentences.japanese: 北は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold in the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 北から来ました。
example_sentences.english: I came from the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]から来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 北の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the north window.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: Evening (夕) plus divination: reading fortunes outside.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing at a slanted gate, half turned away, one foot already off the property. They're not coming in — they're headed the other way, out past the fence and into the open air. That's someone stepping firmly outside.
items.reading_mnemonic: You lock yourself out of Koichi's konbini after hours and a guy named Guy comes tapping the glass from the cold, calling "がい! I'm still stuck out here!" He is very much on the outside.
items.description: Means "outside"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words for the outdoors and things that are external.

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、外国に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Next year, I will go to a foreign country.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、外[がい]国[こく]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は外国人ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is that person a foreigner?
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は外[がい]国[こく]人[ひと]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、外は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold outside today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、外[そと]は寒[さむ]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A blade cutting the way forward, in front of you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a fancy storefront with a wide awning sticking out over the sidewalk and two little legs of a display stand planted underneath. It's the face of the shop — the part that greets you before you ever step inside. That whole shape, the thing you meet first and out in front, means front, or before.
items.reading_mnemonic: A calm Zen monk stands out front of the shop, arriving before everyone else, and he bows and murmurs ぜん as he settles into place. He's always in ぜん — front and center, before the doors open.
items.description: Means front or before; extremely common in words for physical position (in front of) and time (before, previous), such as before an event or the front of a building.

example_sentences.japanese: ここに名前を書きます。
example_sentences.english: I will write my name here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここに名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の午前、病院へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the hospital tomorrow morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の午[ご]前[ぜん]、病[びょう]院[いん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の前で友達を待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait for my friend in front of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]で友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]ちます。

items.mnemonic_text: A small step trailing behind: after and behind.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a runner frozen mid-stride, one leg trailing far behind and a little string dangling off their heel. They're always a step too late, always the one bringing up the rear. Whatever the pack does, this figure comes after — trailing behind.
items.reading_mnemonic: The trailing runner finally staggers across the finish line, dead last, and gasps out a weak "ご... ご..." — trying to say "go" but only managing to arrive after everyone else. That breathless ご is the sound that lands whenever this kanji shows up.
items.description: Means "after" or "behind" and shows up constantly in time words like 午後 (afternoon) and after-related expressions.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の後ろで待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait behind the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の後[うし]ろで待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の午後、図書館に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the library this afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の午[ご]後[ご]、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: これが最後のお菓子です。
example_sentences.english: This is the last snack.
example_sentences.furigana: これが最[さい]後[ご]のお菓[か]子[し]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A marker at the top of the day: noon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the sundial standing on the ground — that single flat line is the earth beneath it. A pole rises up from that ground, and right at the top of the day its shadow points straight down at the line, casting no shadow at all. When the shadow vanishes onto the ground like that, you know it's exactly noon.
items.reading_mnemonic: At high noon a golfer named Gordon lines up his shot and yells "ご!" as he swings, because he can't wait until the sun drops. His voice echoes across the empty midday field: ご, ご, ご.
items.description: Means "noon" or midday; shows up in time words like 午前 (morning/a.m.) and 午後 (afternoon/p.m.).

example_sentences.japanese: 午前は学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]前[ぜん]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 午後は映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I will watch a movie in the afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]後[ご]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日の午前、友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met a friend yesterday morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]の午[ご]前[ぜん]、友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) with a line marking its root: the origin, a book.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a tree standing tall, and then draw the ground right across its trunk — a single flat line marking exactly where the roots meet the soil. That line points to the tree's source, the very origin it grew from. And the thing that captures a story's origin, pressed flat from a tree, is a book.
items.reading_mnemonic: A monk named ほん sits on the mossy steps at Grandma Kane's shrine, reading the same book over and over. Every time a cat brushes past, he mutters "ほん, ほん" without looking up — he cannot put that book down.
items.description: Means book or origin; shows up everywhere, from 本 (book) itself to 日本 (Japan, "origin of the sun").

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read a book every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日本[にほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、日本に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to Japan next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、日本[にほん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日はペンを三本買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought three pens yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]はペンを三[さん]本[ほん]買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Two legs walking: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape: two legs, mid-stride, walking forward and carrying nothing else along with them. That's the whole picture — a body up top, two legs striding out beneath. Two legs walking forward is a person.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jin, the friendly giant, is the biggest person you'll ever meet, ducking through every doorway just to say hello. When you spot this character, picture him waving down at you and hear the giant himself: じん.
items.description: Means "person" and is one of the most common kanji in Japanese, showing up alone and inside countless words for people and nationalities.

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that person over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の友達は外国人です。
example_sentences.english: My friend is a foreigner.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]は外[がい]国[こく]人[ひと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は一人で帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I will go home alone today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は一人[ひとり]で帰[かえ]ります。

items.mnemonic_text: A figure kneeling gracefully: a woman.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at the character and you'll see a figure kneeling gracefully, one arm sweeping across, the other resting low. That elegant kneeling pose is exactly how you were taught to spot a woman.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Jo sweeps into Koichi's konbini and orders in a booming voice, "じょ, that's me!" The whole shelf of onigiri rattles as she says it, so じょ is stuck to this woman for good.
items.description: Means "woman"; a very common N5 kanji that appears in words for females and in compounds relating to girls and women.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女と一緒に映画館へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the cinema with my girlfriend.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that woman?
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の子が公園で遊んでいます。
example_sentences.english: A girl is playing in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の子[こ]が公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んでいます。

items.mnemonic_text: Power (力) worked in the rice field (田): a working man.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a rice field stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his power, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the man.
items.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: だん, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.
items.description: Means "man," and shows up in everyday words for men and boys as well as compounds like 男子; read おとこ on its own and だん in compounds.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that man over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 小さい男の子が犬を見ました。
example_sentences.english: A small boy saw a dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 小[ちい]さい男[おとこ]の子[こ]が犬[いぬ]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 男の人が部屋に入りました。
example_sentences.english: A man entered the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 男[おとこ]の人[ひと]が部屋[へや]に入[い]りました。

items.mnemonic_text: A swaddled baby with arms out: a child.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's a swaddled baby with its little arms flung out to the sides. That bundled shape wriggling and reaching is exactly what this kanji is — a child.
items.reading_mnemonic: A child at the riverbank keeps splashing everyone, so you press a finger to your lips and go "し!" — the sound you make to shush a rowdy kid. That soft "し" is how you hush this child.
items.description: Means "child"; a very common kanji appearing in words for children and as a frequent name ending.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の子は私の弟です。
example_sentences.english: That boy is my younger brother.
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の子[こ]は私[わたし]の弟[おとうと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は新しい帽子を買いました。
example_sentences.english: She bought a new hat.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は新[あたら]しい帽[ぼう]子[し]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日、子供とお菓子を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat sweets with my child every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]、子[こ]供[ども]とお菓[か]子[し]を食[た]べます。

items.mnemonic_text: An upright frame with pupils inside: an eye.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's an upright frame with two pupils sitting inside it. Tip it on its side and it even looks like it's staring right back at you. That frame with pupils is exactly what it is — an eye.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woodcarver named もく is whittling a tiny wooden eye at Koichi's konbini counter, holding it up to inspect the grain. Every time he blinks, he mutters "もく, もく" as he lines the carving up with his own eye.
items.description: Means "eye," the body part; a very common kanji that also shows up in words about looking, sight, and ordering things (as in items on a list).

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の目は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: Her eyes are big.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の目[め]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父は目が悪いです。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather has bad eyesight.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は目[め]が悪[わる]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 自分の目で見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw it with my own eyes.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]の目[め]で見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A dangling shape on the side of the head: an ear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you'll spot a dangling shape hanging off the side of a head. That soft, drooping flap catching every sound is an ear.
items.reading_mnemonic: A jittery DJ named Jiji cups a hand to his ear and shouts "じ, じ, do you hear that beat?" — the sound goes straight into his ear as じ.
items.description: Means "ear"; the body part, and shows up in words about hearing and listening.

example_sentences.japanese: あの犬は耳が大きいです。
example_sentences.english: That dog has big ears.
example_sentences.furigana: あの犬[いぬ]は耳[みみ]が大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの耳は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: The baby's ears are small.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの耳[みみ]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 耳が冷たいです。
example_sentences.english: My ears are cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 耳[みみ]が冷[つめ]たいです。

items.mnemonic_text: An open square: a mouth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character: it's just an open square, a hole with nothing inside. Picture it as a mouth hanging wide open, mid-yawn or mid-shout. An open square, an opening — a mouth.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, leans across the beeping till and shouts an order to his stock boy, his mouth wide open: 「こう!」 Every time he barks like that, you picture that gaping mouth and hear こう.
items.description: Means "mouth" or "opening"; a common N5 kanji that shows up in words about mouths, entrances, and exits.

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの口は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: The baby's mouth is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの口[くち]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 出口はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is the exit?
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the bank's service window.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Fingers and a wrist branching out: a hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you can see the fingers spreading out from a wrist. That's the whole picture: fingers plus a wrist, held up for you to shake. It's a hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A magician named Shu reaches out a bare hand and, with a flick, pulls a coin from behind your ear. As the coin lands in her palm she winks and says, "しゅ, that's all in the hand."
items.description: Means "hand"; a very common kanji that appears in everyday words for hands, gestures, and doing things by hand.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の手は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: His hands are big.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の手[て]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は料理が上手です。
example_sentences.english: My mother is good at cooking.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は料[りょう]理[り]が上手[じょうず]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 郵便局で切手を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a stamp at the post office.
example_sentences.furigana: 郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]で切[きっ]手[て]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth over stopping legs: a foot that carries you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a mouth perched on top of a pair of stopping legs — the legs have skidded to a halt, and the mouth is barking orders down at them. Those legs end in one thing: a foot. That mouth-over-stopping-legs shape is your foot, your leg, the thing you plant when you've had just enough.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named Sok is nursing a blister on her foot. Every painful step she counts out loud, 「そく、そく、そく」, until she finally reaches the vending machine at the top and decides that's enough walking for one day.
items.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は足が長いです。
example_sentences.english: She has long legs.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は足[あし]が長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 足が冷たいです。
example_sentences.english: My feet are cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]が冷[つめ]たいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は足が速いです。
example_sentences.english: Dogs run fast.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は足[あし]が速[はや]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A flexed arm pushing: power and strength.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this single stroke and picture a bent arm flexing hard — the elbow cocked, the muscle bulging. That one flexed arm is all you need to see: it's pure power.
items.reading_mnemonic: A weightlifter named Rio steps up to the bar and gives a warrior's yell as she flexes: "りょく!" The whole gym feels the raw strength in that shout.
items.description: Means power or strength; a common N5 kanji that appears in words about ability, effort, and physical force.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の人は力が強いですね。
example_sentences.english: That man is strong, isn't he?
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は力[ちから]が強[つよ]いですね。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の祖父は力が弱いです。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather doesn't have much strength.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の祖[そ]父[ふ]は力[ちから]が弱[よわ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: テーブルが重いですから、一緒に力を使いましょう。
example_sentences.english: The table is heavy, so let's use our strength together.
example_sentences.furigana: テーブルが重[おも]いですから、一[いっ]緒[しょ]に力[ちから]を使[つか]いましょう。

items.mnemonic_text: A sprout pushing up from the ground: life and birth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single seed pushed into the earth — that cross of soil where everything begins. A green shoot cracks through and reaches up out of the ground. From that patch of earth, something new is born: this is life.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, is the first sprout to shoot up every spring, hand raised before anyone else has even woken. When the teacher asks who's most full of life, Sei（せい）is already standing, beaming.
items.description: Means "life" or "birth"; a very common kanji that shows up in words about living, being born, students, and fresh or raw things.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、駅で先生に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met my teacher at the station yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、駅[えき]で先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生は毎日図書館で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: Students read books at the library every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]は毎[まい]日[にち]図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 去年、妹が生まれました。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister was born last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 去[きょ]年[ねん]、妹[いもうと]が生[う]まれました。

items.mnemonic_text: In the evening (夕) you call out a mouth's (口) name.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Something is missing above the mouth — a marker of who you are. You open your mouth to speak the one word that fills that gap: your name. Every mouth carries a name.
items.reading_mnemonic: A performer named Mei struts into Koichi's konbini and belts out "めい, that's my name, don't wear it out!" She spells it letter by letter until the whole shop knows exactly who she is.
items.description: Means "name"; a very common kanji appearing in words for names, titles, and famous or well-known things.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生の名前は何ですか。
example_sentences.english: What is the teacher's name?
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]の名[な]前[まえ]は何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は有名な医者です。
example_sentences.english: He is a famous doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は有[ゆう]名[めい]な医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あの映画は有名です。
example_sentences.english: That movie is famous.
example_sentences.furigana: あの映[えい]画[が]は有[ゆう]名[めい]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A person carrying grain across one full year.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this whole character and see a scarecrow leaning in a field, arms of straw stretched out, its head tilted from standing there through every season. It has watched the rice grow, get harvested, and grow again — the full turn of the seasons. One complete loop of that scarecrow's silent watch is a year.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tired farmer counts the passing seasons by taking a nap in the shade of that scarecrow each time the harvest ends. He mumbles "ねん、ねん" — like the sleepy sound of nodding off — once for every year that rolls by.
items.description: Means "year"; a very common kanji appearing in dates, ages, and words about time.

example_sentences.japanese: 去年、海に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the sea last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 去[きょ]年[ねん]、海[うみ]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今年、新しいパソコンを買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy a new computer this year.
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]、新[あたら]しいパソコンを買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、兄は大学に行きます。
example_sentences.english: My older brother will go to university next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、兄[あに]は大[だい]学[がく]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) at the temple (寺) marks the hour.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're at the shrine watching the sun climb the sky, day after day, and you realize the sun is nothing but a giant clock. Every time you glance up at that window-with-a-bar, the sun, a whole day has ticked by. That slow, steady march of the sun is how you tell the time.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful clockmaker named Jiro keeps every timepiece in Koichi's konbini ticking, and each hour on the hour he shouts "じ! じ!" as the alarms go off. Whenever you need to know the time, you listen for Jiro's じ.
items.description: Means time or hour, and shows up everywhere you talk about clock time and telling the hour.

example_sentences.japanese: 今は何時ですか。
example_sentences.english: What time is it now?
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]は何[なん]時[じ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい時計を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new watch.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい時計[とけい]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 時々友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I sometimes watch movies with friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 時[とき]々[どき]友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) seen through a gate (門): the space in between.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a gate with its two swinging doors thrown open. Right in the gap between them, the sun is hanging low, filling the opening with light. That sliver of sun caught in the gate is the space between things — an interval, the gap between.
items.reading_mnemonic: A guard named Kan stands watch in that gateway, timing exactly how long the sun lingers in the gap. Every time the interval passes he shouts "かん!" and slams one door shut.
items.description: Means "interval" or "between," the space or gap between two things or times; common in words for time spans and gaps.

example_sentences.japanese: 病院はデパートと駅の間です。
example_sentences.english: The hospital is between the department store and the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 病[びょう]院[いん]はデパートと駅[えき]の間[あいだ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 二時間テレビを見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched TV for two hours.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]時[じ]間[かん]テレビを見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 三週間待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for three weeks.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]週[しゅう]間[かん]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) with wings and birds: naming each day of the week.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You flip your calendar and see the sun, a day, sitting bright at the left edge, while a busy tangle of feathers and squawking birds crowds in beside it. That's how each square is labeled: a sun for the day, plus all the noisy little markings that name it. Each one is a named weekday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Yoko, exhausted, groans "no more, no more" as she crosses off day after day on the wall calendar. Every square she reaches she moans よう, よう, because to her every single weekday feels the same.
items.description: Means "weekday" and appears in the names of the days of the week, as in 月曜日 (Monday) and 日曜日 (Sunday).

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日にデパートで新しい靴を買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy new shoes at the department store on Wednesday.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]にデパートで新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 金曜日の夜は楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: Friday night is fun.
example_sentences.furigana: 金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]の夜[よる]は楽[たの]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日に公園で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read books in the park on Sundays.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a moment held in the hand: now.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot a person walking forward under a wide roof that shelters them from the rain. They don't dwell on where they've been or where they're headed — under that roof, in this exact spot, all that matters is the present moment. A person taking cover means: now.
items.reading_mnemonic: Right now, this very second, Koichi is slamming down onigiri prices at the konbini and yelling "こん!" like a battle cry to get you buying before the moment passes. Every time you hear こん, you know it means now, now, now.
items.description: 今 means "now" and shows up constantly in time words like 今日 (today) and 今 (now) itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 今、私は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、私[わたし]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、友達が家に来ます。
example_sentences.english: A friend is coming to my house today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、友[とも]達[だち]が家[いえ]に来[らい]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今週、映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I will watch a movie this week.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]週[しゅう]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: Making a lap around the calendar road: one week.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a boxy calendar page with a winding path snaking across it, threading from one square to the next through all seven days. You trace that path with your finger, day by day, until it loops right back to where it started. One full loop around that little grid is exactly one week.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Shu (しゅう) plans her whole week on that looping calendar path, and every seven days she sighs "しゅう, another one done!" as she starts the loop again. Hear her say しゅう each time the week resets.
items.description: Means "week"; shows up in everyday time words like 今週 (this week), 毎週 (every week), and 週末 (weekend).

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に友達と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I play with my friends on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy next week.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 先週、新しい本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new book last week.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]週[しゅう]、新[あたら]しい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person over a mother figure repeating every time.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at 毎 as a tightly wound wind-up alarm clock: a fat body with the key twisting out the top and two little feet at the bottom. You crank it up and it goes off the same way, at the same hour, without fail — every single day. That relentless, clockwork repetition is exactly what this character means: every.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clock belongs to Mai, who winds it every morning and shouts "My time!" as it rings. Hear her name まい as the sound that hammers home the routine — every day, まい, まい, まい.
items.description: Means "every" and shows up in common time words for recurring events, such as every day, every week, and every morning.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink coffee every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎晩本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My father reads a book every night.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎月図書館に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the library every month.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]月[つき]図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A shape split evenly down the middle: half.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character straight on: it's a fat exclamation point standing dead center, with two little legs kicked out symmetrically at the top, one left and one right. Those legs split the whole thing right down the middle — perfectly even, one side mirroring the other. Whenever you see something sliced clean into two equal parts, you've found half.
items.reading_mnemonic: Han, the half-and-half chef, holds up a plate where one side is rice and the other is curry, split exactly down the center. "はん!" he barks, tapping the dividing line — because to Han, half is the only portion worth serving.
items.description: Means "half" and shows up constantly in time expressions and portions, like telling the time at half past the hour.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日二時間半勉強します。
example_sentences.english: I study for two and a half hours every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]二[に]時[じ]間[かん]半[はん]勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はこのパンを半分食べます。
example_sentences.english: I will eat half of this bread.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はこのパンを半[はん]分[ぶん]食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 本の半分を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read half of the book.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]の半[はん]分[ぶん]を読[よ]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: A sword (刀) dividing something into parts and minutes.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a knife coming down on a pie, splitting it into eight (the two strokes spreading apart). Each slice is now a part of the whole, and every part is a minute wedge of the original. Once you can split something into its parts like this, you finally understand it: minute, part, understand.
items.reading_mnemonic: A pastry chef at Koichi's konbini slices a cake into perfectly equal parts and blows a "phew" of relief — ふん — when the timer hits one last minute. Every ふん she counts is one more minute closer to closing.
items.description: Means minute, part, or understand; shows up in time expressions (分), in words for portions and parts, and in the verb 分かる, to understand.

example_sentences.japanese: この本は分かりません。
example_sentences.english: I don't understand this book.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は分[わ]かりません。

example_sentences.japanese: パンを半分食べました。
example_sentences.english: I ate half of the bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを半[はん]分[ぶん]食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で五分待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for five minutes at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で五[ご]分[ふん]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: A child (子) under a roof of scattered ideas: study.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a swaddled child, arms out, sitting under a little roof of scribbled notes and diagrams. That's what a child does under that roof all day: they study. A child parked beneath a canopy of lessons is study and learning.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school, the star pupil Gaku is the one who never stops studying, and everyone in the echoing hallways calls out がく whenever they need the answer. Hear がく and you hear the kid who lives to learn.
items.description: Means study or learning; a very common kanji that shows up in words for student, school, and academic subjects.

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は学生です。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister is a student.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to school tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 数学は難しいです。
example_sentences.english: Math is difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: 数[すう]学[がく]は難[むずか]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) crossed with mingling students: a school.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single tree standing in the middle of a courtyard, its trunk, roots, and branches spreading over a crowd of kids at recess. Every institution built around that one old tree runs on the same schedule: bells, classrooms, homework. A tree at the heart of the yard means school.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, has set up a pop-up shop right inside the school gate, restocking onigiri between classes and muttering こう, こう as he lines up the shelves. The kids buy their lunch from him before the bell.
items.description: Means "school"; shows up in everyday words for schools and school life, such as 学校.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 校庭に犬がいます。
example_sentences.english: There is a dog in the schoolyard.
example_sentences.furigana: 校[こう]庭[てい]に犬[いぬ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、学校を休みます。
example_sentences.english: I will take a day off from school today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A person stepping ahead of the rest: previous and first.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot two legs left standing without a body, striding out the door ahead of everyone else. No torso to slow them down — those legs are always one step in front, gone before you've even moved. Whatever they're doing, they did it previous to you and they're already ahead.
items.reading_mnemonic: Those bodiless legs sprint down the mountain trail so far ahead they trip a wire and set off a whole line of fireworks — せん, せん, せん — bursting one after another to mark how far in front they already are.
items.description: Means previous or ahead; shows up in words about coming before, like 先生 (teacher, literally "born before") and 先週 (last week).

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、先生に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met the teacher yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先週、友達と一緒に映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a movie with a friend last week.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]週[しゅう]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先月、新しい靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought new shoes last month.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]月[げつ]、新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Speech (言) with a mouth counting to five (五): words and language.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the left, words/speech is already pouring out — a mouth releasing stacked lines of speech. On the right, another open mouth joins in, adding its own noise. When mouths keep stacking speech on top of speech like this, what you get is a whole language, packed with word after word.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini, a chatty regular named Go won't stop talking — every single language pours out of him at once, and the only word you catch is his own name, ご, ご, ご.
items.description: Means language or word; shows up in words like 日本語 (Japanese language) and 英語 (English), and read かた in 物語 (story).

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と日本語で話します。
example_sentences.english: I speak with my friend in Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と日本[にほん]語[ご]で話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: この本は英語です。
example_sentences.english: This book is in English.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は英[えい]語[ご]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日日本語を勉強します。
example_sentences.english: I study Japanese every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

items.mnemonic_text: Speech (言) plus a tongue (舌): telling a story.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A mouth releasing stacked lines of speech leans in close, and right beside it a tongue sticks out of a mouth, wagging nonstop. Put the speech next to the busy tongue and you've got someone who just won't stop talking, spinning story after story.
items.reading_mnemonic: Wanda the storyteller loves an audience, so she waves both hands and calls out "わ!" every time she starts a new tale. That little "わ" is her signal that another long talk is about to begin.
items.description: Means talk or story; shows up in everyday words for speaking, conversation, and telephone.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と話します。
example_sentences.english: I will talk with my friend tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい電話を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new phone.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい電[でん]話[わ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生の話は面白いです。
example_sentences.english: The teacher's story is interesting.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]の話[はなし]は面[おも]白[しろ]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) sold (売) to your eyes: reading.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the right, a merchant is hawking his wares, and next to him stands words and speech, that mouth stacking line after line into the air. But the merchant isn't selling — he's leaning in, eyes moving down the columns of speech, drinking in every line. He isn't listening; he's there to read.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reader you find hunched over those lines of speech is a poison-pen critic, and you nickname her Doku (どく) because every review she reads she then tears apart. Watch her read a page and you can practically see the どく venom drip off her pen.
items.description: Means "read"; the core kanji in 読む (to read) and in words like 読書 (reading books).

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日本を読みます。
